concepts.title: Index Number Meaning and Uses
concepts.definition: An index number is a percentage-relative measure that shows how a variable, such as a price level, changes between a base period (index 100) and the current period. Index numbers of prices, quantities and values are called economic barometers because they summarise whole markets in one figure.
concepts.key_idea: Index 100 is the base. An index of 125 means the level rose 25 percent over the base; 92 means a fall of 8 percent. Uses include cost-of-living adjustments, policy framing and deflating nominal series into real ones.
question_patterns: The price of a commodity rose from {base} to {cur}; find the price index with the base year as 100.
An index moves from 100 to {idx}; state the percentage change.
What is an index number and why is it called an economic barometer?
If the cost-of-living index is {idx}, how has the price level changed from the base year?
State two uses of index numbers in economics.

concepts.title: Simple Aggregative Price Index
concepts.definition: The simple aggregative method adds up the prices of all commodities in the current year and divides by the sum of their base-year prices, multiplying by 100. It ignores quantity weights, so dearer commodities dominate the movement.
concepts.key_idea: Strength: simple to compute from totals alone. Weakness: the units and the importance of items are ignored, which is why weighted methods are preferred in practice.
question_patterns: Prices of three items in the base year are {a}, {b}, {c} and in the current year {d}, {e}, {f}; find the simple aggregative index.
Compute the unweighted aggregative price index for the given data.
State one limitation of the simple aggregative method.
The sum of base prices is {sum_base} and of current prices is {sum_cur}; find the index number.
Why can one costly item distort the simple aggregative index?

concepts.title: Laspeyres Price Index
concepts.definition: The Laspeyres index is the weighted aggregative index that uses base-year quantities as weights: the ratio of the current cost of the base-year basket to its base-year cost, times 100. It answers how the old basket's price has moved.
concepts.key_idea: Weights stay frozen at base-year consumption, so the index is unaffected by new buying habits but may overstate inflation by ignoring substitution away from dearer goods.
question_patterns: Using base-year quantities {q1}, {q2} and prices (base {p1b}, {p2b}; current {p1c}, {p2c}), find the Laspeyres index.
Define the Laspeyres price index and state which quantities weight it.
Find the current cost of the base-year basket given the data.
Why does the Laspeyres index tend to overstate price rises?
Compute L = sum(p1 q0) / sum(p0 q0) * 100 for the given table.

concepts.title: Paasche Price Index
concepts.definition: The Paasche index is the weighted aggregative index that uses current-year quantities as weights: the current cost of the current basket over what that same basket would have cost at base-year prices, times 100.
concepts.key_idea: Weights update every year with current consumption, so the index reflects present buying habits but tends to understate inflation and needs fresh quantity data each period.
question_patterns: Using current-year quantities {q1}, {q2} with base prices {p1b}, {p2b} and current prices {p1c}, {p2c}, find the Paasche index.
Define the Paasche price index and name its weights.
Contrast the weights used by Laspeyres and Paasche indices.
Compute sum(p1 q1) / sum(p0 q1) * 100 for the given data.
Why does the Paasche index need new quantity data every year?

concepts.title: Tests of Adequacy Unit and Time Reversal
concepts.definition: Adequacy tests check index formulae. The unit test demands that the index be independent of the units of measurement. The time-reversal test demands that the index swapping base and current years be reciprocals: P01 times P10 should equal 1, so an index forward of 125 must pair with 80 backward.
concepts.key_idea: Laspeyres and Paasche each fail the time-reversal test separately; their geometric mean, Fisher's ideal index, passes both the time-reversal and factor-reversal tests.
question_patterns: Check whether P01 = {l} and P10 = {pidx} satisfy the time-reversal test.
State the time-reversal test for index numbers.
Which index number formula is called ideal and why?
Show that the simple aggregative index satisfies the unit test.
If the forward index is {l}, what backward index does the time-reversal test require?

concepts.title: Time Series and Linear Trend
concepts.definition: A time series records a variable across ordered time periods, combining trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular components. The linear trend line y = a + b x is fitted by least squares, and when the number of years is even the x-origin is shifted to the midpoint between the two middle years in half-year units.
concepts.key_idea: The slope b gives the average change per unit of x (per year, or per half-year when the origin is mid-interval); substituting a coded x forecasts the trend value for that period.
question_patterns: Fit a linear trend to the given sales data and interpret the slope.
The trend line is y = {a} + {b}x; find the trend value at x = {x}.
Name the four components of a time series.
Why is the origin shifted to the midpoint when the number of years is even?
Using the trend line y = {a} + {b}x, forecast the value one period ahead of x = {x}.

worked_examples.q: Base-year prices of wheat, rice and oil are 20, 30 and 50; current prices are 24, 33 and 60. Find the simple aggregative index.
worked_examples.a: Sum of base prices = 20 + 30 + 50 = 100. Sum of current prices = 24 + 33 + 60 = 117. Index = 117 / 100 x 100 = 117, so the price level rose 17 percent over the base year.

worked_examples.q: Laspeyres index is 125 and the Paasche index for the same data is 80. Do these satisfy the time-reversal test?
worked_examples.a: The test needs P01 x P10 = 1. Here 1.25 x 0.80 = 1.00, so yes: the forward index 125 and backward index 80 are reciprocals, since 125/100 times 80/100 equals 1.
